newsitem.title: FRANCE: Just surviving isn't enough for new Apple chief.
newsitem.headline: Just surviving isn't enough for new Apple chief.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc chairman Gil Amelio said on Thursday the loss-making company would forge new alliances in a bid to recapture its glory days as an innovative maverick of the computer industry.
"Apple will survive, but survival is not good enough," Amelio told reporters in Paris the day after the company struck a deal with Sun Microcomputers Inc.
In Paris for the Apple Expo show for partners and customers, Amelio hosted a lunch to outline the strategy for the company that appointed him chairman and chief executive in February.
"We had a tough time but we are coming out of it. Now we have to become a winner again," Amelio said.

Under the deal with Sun, Apple computers will be linked to Sun servers to give business clients an alternative to Microsoft Corp's Windows NT platform running on machines powered by Intel Corp's Pentium chips.
Apple has its own operating system to run Macintosh computers and uses the PowerPC chip developed by Motorola Inc, IBM Corp and Cie des Machines Bull.
But while striving to counter the "WIntel" dominance, Amelio said that in essence the "war of the operating systems is over".

He explained that with the Internet, there was a new class of software, called middleware, which communicates between machines over networks. Browers, multimedia software like QuickTime and Sun's Java are such middleware.
Amelio said he expected the three-year product development deal with Sun to be extended for at least three more years.
He called the war between Netscape Communications Corp and Microsoft for dominance of the browser software market to access information over the Internet outdated.
People did not really want to browse on the Internet but rather get information they can use. That too will be the job of middleware.
Amelio, 52, said Apple under his leadership would focus less on hardware and more on software.
"In the past, we made software in order to sell hardware. Now we must make software to create value for our customers," he said.
Gesticulating, he tried to convince his audience Apple had taken a new, more realistic course after amking big losses.
"Maybe once in a lifetime you can develop a software programme that will change the world. But at Apple, our creative people tried to do that every Tuesday," he said.
Amelio said he had already improved Apple's financial position, and aimed to "meet or beat" his forecast of breaking even in the first quarter of 1997 -- the second fiscal quarter for Apple.
The company posted losses of $740 million in the second quarter of this year.
The Apple Macintosh, for long a closed system, has been opened to clone makers but Amelio aims to go further and use as many "commodity" hardware components as possible.
